newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Central/east European stocks have buoyant week.
newsitem.headline: Central/east European stocks have buoyant week.

text.p: Share prices on central and east European bourses moved upwards across the board this week, reaching highs in Prague, Warsaw and Bratislava.

The Central European Share Index (CESI), which reflects price movements in 73 Polish, Czech, Hungarian, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, edged higher over the week to close at a new record high of 1,726.32 points.
PRAGUE
Spectacular gains for the PX50's biggest banking issue, Komercni Banka, spurred the index on to a new 12-month high of 613.4 on Thursday with dealers seeing further advances in the coming sessions.

Komercni, which has risen nearly 10 percent since the beginning of the week, was pushed up by strong long term arbitrage possibilities existing between Komercni's price on the Prague bourse, 2,905 at Thursday's close, and its global depositary receipt price in London, currently 3,446.
WARSAW

The Warsaw Stock Exchange edged up 0.2 percent this week, setting a 35-month high on Tuesday, but analysts expected it to fall in profit-taking next week after having gained about 38 percent since mid-December.

"All ratios of technical analysis are overheated and show sell-signals, companies earnings reports for January were not spectacular, so surely the correction will happen," said Pawel Dmytryk, a trader at Bank Staropolski brokerage.

Some analysts said the expected profit-taking could last about a month but Poland's good economic prospects and expanding possibilities such as new issues and forthcoming large privatisations were attracting new foreign capital, which could later push the WIG index up.
BUDAPEST

Hungarian share prices edged a shade higher through the week as bourse-listed companies completed the publication of their preliminary 1996 earnings reports. On Thursday the BUX index finished at 5,578.73 points, up 58.33 from last Friday.
"The market reached the end of an expansive period and investors will now review what to invest in," one trader said.
The share market has calmed down and investors were waiting for the planned new phase of a selloff in oil company MOL.
BRATISLAVA

The Bratislava Stock Exchange (BSE) extended last week's uptrend with four consecutive year highs this week. Brokers said the gains may continue due to strong demand for still undervalued blue chips and high interbank market rates prompting foreign capital to turn to the stock market.
The 16-share SAX index rose 5.28 points from Monday's opening, or 2.68 percent, to close at 201.95 points on Thursday.

"In principle, blue chips are rising and trading has become more lively as currently higher interbank money market rates had attracted some foreign capital inflow," Vladimir Kuklis, a CSOB Bank analyst said. "It appears that the trend will continue for a while."
ZAGREB

Croatian stocks were mixed in slower trade on Thursday after recovering most of their lost ground earlier in the week and market participants expected stagnation unless foreign investors step in to prop up trade.
"It is hard to say what any of the big buyers are up to," said Marko Nikolac at Metroholding brokerage.
He singled out Kras chocolate maker, gaining 15 kuna this week on relatively large volumes, as having good prospects.
The company said it was near closing an investment deal with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
LJUBLJANA

Slovenian shares rose 2.5 percent by Thursday's close as the blue-chip SBI index added 34.7 points to 1,404.1. Pharmaceuticals trader Salus outperformed the market, rising 14.9 percent, while financial consultancy Primofin bucked the trend, plummeting 13 percent.
BUCHAREST
Heavy trading in first-tier stocks Azomures SA fertiliser maker and chemical plant Oltchim SA, which joined the market on Tuesday, kept turnover on the Bucharest bourse high this week.
Demand outrunning supply sent the bulk of prices up on Thursday, when the independent VAB and BIG indices hit year highs.
TIRANA
For the second consecutive week, neither T-bills nor bonds were traded on the dormant Tirana Stock Exchange during its two weekly sessions on Monday and Thursday.
"Two banks are really taking care to preserve their liquidity now since the lek is weakening," said a trader.

The local currency has hit a record low of about 130 leks to the dollar, having dropped some 25 percent since the start of the year as Albania plunged into its biggest political and financial crisis since the fall of communism six years ago.
The collapse of several fraudulent investment schemes in January left many Albanians penniless and has stirred weeks of popular unrest across the country.
The right-wing government of President Sali Berisha has promised help to some of the hardest-hit investors but has insisted that it will not print money to bail them out.
